title: Read the Street
subtitle: A field guide to observing public space
purpose: Help a first-time observer take grounded field notes and write one defensible observation about how a public place is used.
audience: Adult design and planning students on a first field visit

criteria: Distinguish observation from interpretation using the same public seating example throughout.
Keep the field routine, comparison, practice steps and checklist editable.

blocks.label: Field guide
blocks.lead: A bench, an awning and a busy crossing can tell you where people pause and how they move. Spend twenty minutes watching one stretch of a public street and turn what you see into an observation someone else could check.
blocks.caption: Bring a notebook, a watch and one question about how the place is used.

blocks.text: Pick one corner, bus stop or entrance. Keep the same boundary for both observation periods and write down where you stood, the time and the weather.

blocks.title: Start with a question you can answer by watching
blocks.text: Try “Where do people stop while they wait?” Mark seating, shelter and the edge of the walking route before you count any stops.

steps.label: Minutes 0–5 · Map
steps.detail: Sketch your boundary and mark fixed features. Choose a visible point where you can observe without blocking the path.

steps.label: Minutes 5–15 · Count
steps.detail: Make a tally each time someone stops for more than ten seconds. Mark each stop on the sketch.

steps.label: Minutes 15–20 · Check
steps.detail: Rescan the same boundary. Record a change such as a shower starting or a bus arriving and keep the counts from the two periods separate.

blocks.text: Record movement and use of space in aggregate. Leave names, faces and other identifying details out of the notes.
Write the observation first. If you have an explanation, label it as a hypothesis and name something you could check on a second visit.

blocks.caption: Two sentences about the same place
rows: Six of the eight people who stopped waited under the awning. Light rain began at 12:14.
People may choose the awning when it rains. Repeat the count from the same spot on a dry day.

blocks.title: Try it on your own notes
blocks.intro: Select one pattern from your map. Use only observations within the boundary you set at the start.
steps: Write one sentence giving the count, location and time.
Write a separate sentence with an explanation and one way to check it.

items: The count and units are explicit.
The two sentences separate evidence and explanation.
Another observer could repeat the check.

blocks.title: What to carry forward
blocks.text: Keep the map and the count alongside your claim so the next visit can confirm it or change it.
